imp.generic: Boredom is an unpleasant feeling that most people try to avoid.
imp.author: Boredom is not, it turns out, the absence of feeling—which is what you assume before you have really been bored, before you have sat in the particular nowhere of a Tuesday afternoon with nothing due and nowhere to be and discovered that boredom is itself a feeling, a thick and almost physical one, like being upholstered from the inside, and that what it most resembles, in its texture and its weight, is dread, which is interesting, which is the kind of thing you would find interesting if you were not, right now, so completely and annihilatingly bored.

imp.generic: The average American checks their phone eighty-six times per day.
imp.author: The average American checks their phone eighty-six times per day, which is a statistic that will make you look at your phone, which you are possibly holding right now, which means the statistic is not really a statistic so much as a mirror, and the face looking back is doing the thing the statistic describes, is in fact doing it at this precise moment of reading about doing it, and the recursion here is not accidental, is in fact the whole point, is the thing that keeps certain people—people who think about this kind of thing, people who cannot stop thinking about this kind of thing—awake at 3 a.m. with the phone face-down on the nightstand, glowing faintly, patient, waiting.

imp.generic: She realized, driving home, that she was deeply unhappy.
imp.author: What she understood, somewhere on the interchange between the 405 and the 10, in the particular nowhere of a merge, was not that she was unhappy—the word was too small, too clinical, a word for surveys—but that she had been performing happiness for so long, with such technical proficiency, that she had lost the ability to distinguish the performance from whatever was supposed to be underneath it, and that this, the not-knowing, the suspicion that there was no underneath, that she had performed all the way down, was the actual thing, the real texture of what she was, and the horror of it was not that it was unbearable but that it was, in fact, completely bearable, that she would bear it, that she was already bearing it, that she would stop for gas and then go home.

imp.generic: This is a story about a man who could not stop apologizing.
imp.author: The thing you need to understand about Gary—and understanding Gary will require some patience, some willingness to sit with a person who is, on the surface, not particularly interesting, which is itself a thing Gary would apologize for—is that Gary's apologies were not, as his second wife maintained, a form of aggression, a way of making the apologized-to feel monstrous for accepting them; they were, or had started as, genuine, which is somehow worse, which is the part of Gary's story that makes it, if you are willing to stay with it, not about Gary at all.

imp.generic: Furthermore, it is important to consider the role that loneliness plays in modern life.
imp.author: And here is where we have to talk about loneliness, which I have been avoiding, which you may have noticed I have been avoiding, because loneliness is one of those words that has been used so many times in so many contexts—the loneliness of the crowd, the loneliness of the long-distance runner, the loneliness of the human condition, which phrase alone should be retired, should be taken out behind the shed—that it has been sanded down to almost nothing, and yet the thing it points at, the actual experience, which is not sadness exactly and not solitude exactly but something more like the specific ache of being a self that cannot be fully transferred to another self no matter how long or hard you try, that thing is as real as ever, is in fact, in 2024, with all the connectivity and the feeds and the notifications, possibly more real than ever, which is the part nobody wants to say out loud at the dinner party, so I am saying it here, in a footnote, where it is easier.

imp.generic: He tried to explain how much he loved her, but the words felt inadequate.
imp.author: What he wanted to say—and he was aware, saying it, of how many people had wanted to say exactly this, how worn the path was, how the very universality of the feeling was part of what made it so hard to say without sounding like a greeting card or a man who had learned about love from greeting cards—was that she was the only person in whose presence he did not feel the low-grade, nearly subsonic hum of performance, the sense of being watched and evaluated and found either sufficient or insufficient, and that this, the silence of that hum, was the closest thing to peace he had ever found, and that he was aware this was not a romantic thing to say, was possibly the least romantic thing he had ever said, and that he was saying it anyway, out loud, in the car, with the radio off, because it was true, which was the only thing he had.

imp.generic: The meeting ended, and everyone filed out of the conference room.
imp.author: The meeting ended the way meetings end—not with resolution, not with the crisp narrative click of a thing concluded, but with a kind of thermodynamic winding-down, a trailing off of the agenda into the meta-agenda of scheduling the next meeting, and then the gathering of laptops and the performance of purposefulness, everyone suddenly very busy, very somewhere-to-be, and the fluorescent lights above the conference table continued to hum at their particular frequency, indifferent, and the whiteboard still had the diagram on it, the one with the arrows, the one nobody had explained, and it would stay there until Thursday when Facilities would erase it, and whatever it meant, if it meant anything, would be gone.

imp.generic: Grief does not follow a predictable timeline.
imp.author: What the pamphlets—and there are pamphlets, handed to you in the beige office with the box of tissues positioned at the exact angle of maximum implication—what the pamphlets do not tell you is that grief is not a process, not a series of stages you move through like levels in a game, collecting your denial and your anger and your acceptance like coins, but is instead a climate, a thing you live inside, and that the days when you forget, when you go a whole afternoon without the knowledge sitting on your sternum, are not progress but are themselves a kind of grief, a grief about the forgetting, a missing of the missing, and that you will feel guilty about the forgetting, and then guilty about the guilt, and that this is not pathology, this is just what it is, this is the texture of the thing, and no pamphlet is going to tell you that because no pamphlet has figured out how to say it without sounding like it is making things worse, which it would be, which this is, which I am sorry about.

imp.generic: There is something uniquely uncomfortable about being praised in public.
imp.author: Public praise—the toast, the award, the moment when someone stands and says your name and the room turns—is a species of suffering that has no socially acceptable name, which is part of what makes it so difficult, because you cannot, in the moment of being celebrated, explain that what you are experiencing is a kind of exposure, a being-seen that is not the same as being known, that the applause is for a version of you that you yourself do not entirely recognize, a you assembled from your most legible qualities and presented back to you as though it were the whole, and you smile, you are smiling right now in this hypothetical, you are doing the humble-grateful face you have practiced without knowing you were practicing it, and somewhere behind the face the real you is watching the performed you receive the praise, and the real you is not moved, is in fact faintly nauseated, and the gap between those two yous is the loneliest place in the room, which is a room full of people who wish you well, which is the part that gets you, later, alone.

imp.generic: In the end, he was not sure any of it had mattered.
imp.author: And maybe this is the thing, the actual thing, the one you keep not-quite-arriving at: not that it didn't matter—because it did, it does, the mattering is not in question, you can feel the mattering the way you feel a tooth with your tongue—but that mattering and meaning are not the same thing, that a life can be full of the former and still leave you, at the end of a day or a decade, unable to construct a sentence that begins 'the point was,' and that this inability is not failure, is not evidence of a life mis-spent, but is maybe just what it is to be a person, to be this specific and temporary arrangement of wanting and trying and falling short and trying again, and that the wanting to have it mean something, the reaching for the sentence, is itself—if you are willing to let it be, if you can stand to let it be—enough, or close enough, or the closest thing to enough that any of us are going to get, which is not nothing, which is, on the better days, almost everything.
